article.title: Why a Higher Conversion Rate Can Still Produce Fewer Customers

paragraphs.en:
Conversion rate is one of the most common business metrics because it summarizes efficiency in a simple percentage. If 1,000 eligible customers receive an offer and 50 convert, the conversion rate is 5 percent. If the rate later rises to 6 percent, it is tempting to conclude that performance improved. But a higher rate can coexist with fewer actual customers.

The reason is simple: conversions equal the eligible population multiplied by the conversion rate. Suppose last year 100,000 customers were eligible and 5 percent converted. That produces 5,000 conversions. This year targeting becomes narrower, so only 70,000 customers are eligible. Even if conversion rises to 6 percent, the result is 4,200 conversions. Efficiency improved, but volume fell.

This distinction matters in marketing, lending, subscriptions, recruiting, and many other settings. A model may become better at selecting high-propensity customers while excluding a large middle group. Reported CVR rises because the denominator becomes stronger, not necessarily because the intervention itself became more persuasive.

The reverse can also happen. A company expands eligibility to weaker prospects. Conversion rate falls from 6 percent to 5 percent, but the eligible population doubles. Total conversions may rise substantially. Calling this deterioration based only on CVR would miss the business outcome.

Analysts should therefore report rates and counts together. A useful funnel shows eligible population, contacted population, responders or applicants, conversions, and the conversion rate between relevant stages. When the rate changes, ask whether the numerator changed, the denominator changed, or both.

Selection rules deserve special attention. If this year's campaign uses a higher model-score threshold than last year's, the two CVRs describe different populations. A direct comparison mixes campaign effectiveness with audience composition. Stable cohorts, score bands, stratified reporting, or experimental designs can help separate these effects.

Capacity constraints create another trade-off. A sales team may be able to contact only 20,000 leads. In that case, maximizing conversion among those contacts can be valuable even if the broader eligible population is larger. The correct metric depends on the decision: efficiency per contact, total customers acquired, profit, or incremental conversions.

Costs also matter. Acquiring 5,000 customers at a 5 percent CVR may be less profitable than acquiring 4,200 at 6 percent if the second strategy sharply reduces contact costs or attracts higher-value customers. Rate and count are necessary but not always sufficient; unit economics and customer value may change the conclusion.

This is why dashboards should avoid presenting a percentage without its denominator. A 20 percent increase in CVR sounds impressive, but the business interpretation is incomplete until we know the population size and selection process. The same principle applies to defect rates, churn rates, approval rates, and response rates.

A strong business explanation might say: “CVR improved from 5 percent to 6 percent, but the eligible population fell by 30 percent, so conversions decreased from 5,000 to 4,200.” That sentence preserves both efficiency and scale. The broader lesson is simple: a rate tells us how often something happens within a defined population; it does not tell us how large that population is. To understand the outcome, always read the percentage together with its denominator and absolute count.
paragraphs.zh: 轉換率是效率指標，不等於轉換人數。轉換人數＝母數×CVR，因此母數縮小時，即使 CVR 上升，最終轉換人數仍可能下降。比較年度或活動時，還要檢查 targeting 規則、score threshold 與客群構成是否改變。最好的報告方式是同時呈現 eligible population、各 funnel 人數、CVR 與實際轉換數，必要時再加入成本與 customer value。
paragraphs.ja: CVRは効率を表す率であり、契約者数そのものではありません。契約者数は母数×CVRで決まるため、対象母数が縮小すればCVRが上がっても実数は減り得ます。年度比較では対象条件やスコア閾値、顧客構成の変化も確認し、率・分母・実数をセットで示すことが重要です。
